title: An implicit curve and level set: where is f(x, y) = c?
summary: Contour lines of a function of two variables, each labelled with its value. Where the level changes character (a critical level) the topology of the curve changes, and the plot highlights that level.

media.alt: Contour lines of x^4 - 2x^2 + 2y^2 in blue with value labels, a thick orange figure-eight at the critical level c = 0, a rose dot at the saddle in the middle and teal triangles at the two minima.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where is f(x, y) = c?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y are the two inputs (-2 to 2 and -1.6 to 1.6) with equal scale. There is no third axis: the value of f is carried by which contour line you are on, named by its label. Thick amber line: the critical level c = 0.
look_at: Count the closed loops at c = -0.8 and at c = 1. One level has two separate loops and the other has one.
Where do the two loops merge? At the saddle (rose dot) on the critical contour c = 0.
Where are contours closest together? There the function changes fastest.
Which side of a contour is higher? Labels tell you; the lines alone do not.
as_drawn: Levels drawn: -0.8, -0.4, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, plus the critical level 0 in thick amber with the label 'c = 0 (critical)'.
The minima at (plus or minus 1, 0), where f = -1, are marked with teal triangles; the saddle at the origin, f = 0, with a rose dot.
The scale is equal on both axes. The levels are not evenly spaced in c, which is why the gap between lines does not directly show the gradient.
read_the_figure.proves: Where the chosen levels lie and how their shape changes, including the merger at c = 0. It does not prove there are no other features between the drawn levels.
if_wrong: Unlabelled lines: direction of increase unknown, minima and maxima cannot be told apart.
Levels chosen at even steps that skip the critical value: the topology change is missed.
Unequal axis scales: loops that are circles in the plane look like ellipses.

terms.meaning: All points where f takes one value c; a curve in the plane.
The drawing of a level set; also called an isoline.
The vector of partial derivatives; it points uphill and is perpendicular to contours.
A point where the gradient is zero: minimum, maximum or saddle.
A critical point that is a minimum in one direction and a maximum in another. Contours cross there.
The matrix of second derivatives. Its signs classify critical points.

remember: Contours never cross, except at a saddle.
Closely packed contours mean a large gradient.
Label the levels; mark the critical level.
Gradient is perpendicular to contours and points to higher c.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position carries the plane. Each blue line is one level set of f and its label gives c; the thick amber line is the level where the shape changes; marker shapes and colours name the minima and the saddle. The value of f is therefore carried by label and by which line you are on, not by an axis.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A function of two variables lives in three dimensions, but a flat page can show the cuts at chosen heights. A cut at height c is exactly the set where f = c, so a contour plot is a stack of height cuts viewed from above, as on a map. The merger at c = 0 appears as two loops joining at a point: the saddle.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A contour plot shows nothing between the chosen levels. Evenly spaced levels can miss a critical value. Without labels you cannot tell which side is higher. A finite grid can create spurious wiggles near sharp features. And equal packing of lines in a place where the levels are unevenly spaced misleads the eye about the gradient.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Labels give the value, so the reader knows direction and size. The highlighted critical level shows where the structure changes; it must be computed (here from the gradient), not guessed. Together they say what the picture means.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A filled contour plot with a colour bar shows the value everywhere but hides exact levels. A surface plot shows height but hides what is behind a ridge. A gradient arrow field (F2.4) adds direction. For one implicit curve and nothing else, draw only that line.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Overlay the gradient direction as short arrows crossing each contour at right angles, and fill the region f < 0 lightly to show the two basins.

steps.title: Find the critical points
steps.note: f(0, 0) = 0 and f(plus or minus 1, 0) = -1. Those two values are the critical levels.

steps.title: Classify with the Hessian
steps.note: Mixed signs mean a saddle, both positive a minimum. Level c < -1 is empty; -1 < c < 0 two loops; c > 0 one loop.

steps.title: The critical contour
steps.note: A figure-eight: it reaches x = plus or minus sqrt 2 = 1.41 on the axis and, at x = 1, y = plus or minus 0.71, matching the amber curve.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) how many loops at c = -0.8 and at c = 1? (2) How wide is the critical curve? (3) Where is the function changing fastest?

solution.text: c = -0.8 gives two small separate loops around the minima; c = 1 gives one loop around both.
The amber curve reaches x of about plus or minus 1.4 on the axis, which is sqrt 2.
Contours are closest at the left and right outer edges. The gradient size confirms:

worked.answer: Two loops below the critical level, one above; the critical contour is a figure-eight of half-width 1.41; the steepest region is out at large |x|.

analyze.q: Why can two contours of different levels never cross except at a saddle?
analyze.hint: A point has one value of f.

analyze.q: What would the plot look like if the levels were evenly spaced from -1 to 4?
If you saw closed loops with labels increasing inwards, what critical point lies at the centre?

evaluate.q: A contour plot of measured data shows many small closed loops. Are they features or noise, and how would you decide?
evaluate.hint: Compare the loop size with the grid spacing and the noise level.

create: Choose the levels of a contour plot from the critical values of f instead of an even grid.
Add the gradient field as arrows and check that every arrow crosses the contours at 90 degrees.

checks.q: What is the shape of the level set f = c as c rises through the saddle value?
checks.hint: Think of water filling two basins.
checks.answer: Two separate loops merge into one at the saddle level, then one loop surrounds both.

checks.q: Evaluate f(x, y) = x^4 - 2x^2 + 2y^2 at (1, 0) and decide whether it is a minimum.
checks.answer: f = -1, gradient zero, Hessian diag(8, 4) positive: a minimum.

checks.q: A contour plot looks like it has a single basin, yet the function has two. What went wrong?
checks.answer: The drawn levels all lie above the saddle value, so only the merged loop is visible; add levels below the saddle, including the critical one.
